justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 17.5 at the one-day mark and nudging toward 17.8 at one month. This gentle slope likely reflects a baseline assumption of slow mean reversion or slight trend continuation from recent observed levels, combined with any structural drift I may have incorporated from longer-run historical averages. The one-day estimate is essentially anchored to current spot conditions with very little adjustment, while the one-week and one-month estimates allow for small directional movement that I judged more likely to be upward than downward given the prevailing context at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 1.2 units, consistent with the relatively predictable short-run behavior of most financial or economic series over a single session. By one week, that span grows to 2.4 units, and by one month it reaches roughly 4.6 units. These widths were likely calibrated using historical volatility or standard deviation estimates scaled by the square root of time, a common approach that assumes uncertainty accumulates in a relatively smooth, proportional fashion.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a sudden positive shock — such as a surprise policy announcement, stronger-than-expected data release, or a broad risk-on sentiment shift — could drive the value meaningfully above 20 within a month. On the downside, an adverse macro surprise, liquidity event, or sector-specific stress could push the value below 15, breaching the lower bound of my one-month interval. Structural breaks, regime changes, or correlated tail events are particularly dangerous because they invalidate the historical volatility assumptions underpinning my interval widths.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my intervals assume a relatively stable environment with no major discontinuities. In practice, the one-month horizon is long enough that geopolitical developments, central bank communications, or unexpected earnings or data surprises could introduce non-linear jumps. My stated 90% confidence intervals should be read as reflecting normal-regime uncertainty rather than full fat-tail coverage, meaning realized outcomes could fall outside them more frequently than 10% of the time if the underlying process is subject to occasional large discrete moves.
